findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into root shell at build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever the remote server returns as root during `docker build`. There is no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and `-sL` silently follows redirects, so the fetched content can change at any time (or be swapped by a compromised host/DNS/MITM) and immediately run arbitrary code in the image, tainting every downstream artifact built from it. The failure is unreproducible and undetectable at review time because the payload is not part of the repo.

findings.title: Avoid curl|sh of unverified remote script in build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes arbitrary remote content at image-build time with no integrity or version guarantee: there is no checksum/signature verification, no pinned version/commit, and no `-f` so an HTTP error body (or empty output) is piped straight into `sh`. Any compromise, move, or takeover of that URL — or a silent non-2xx response — yields unreviewed code running as root in the build, non-deterministically and non-reproducibly. This is the classic unpinned remote-execution supply-chain risk on a path that publishes the final image.

findings.title: Remove unpinned remote script executed at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: The added layer pipes a script fetched from a mutable remote URL (https://example.com/install.sh) directly into a root shell during `docker build`. There is no commit/tag pin, no checksum or signature verification, and no TLS-to-content binding, so any change, hijack, or DNS/MITM on that URL yields arbitrary root code execution inside the image and every image built from it. Builds are non-reproducible and cannot be audited: the same Dockerfile can silently produce different, potentially compromised images over time.

findings.title: Pipeline discards curl failure, build continues with no install
findings.whyItBreaks: In `RUN curl -sL <url> | sh` the step's exit status is that of `sh` (last command in the pipeline); there is no `pipefail` in the default `/bin/sh`, and `curl -sL` lacks `-f`, so `curl` also exits 0 on HTTP 4xx/5xx. If the fetch fails (network error, DNS failure, 404, empty body), `sh` receives empty/HTML stdin, does nothing, and exits 0 — the `RUN` layer reports success while the intended install silently never happened, producing a broken image that fails later in non-obvious ways.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault hides ErrMissing behind an empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards the error returned by Load (line 16) and returns only the zero value. Callers can no longer distinguish "key absent" (ErrMissing) from "key present with an empty value": both yield "". The function is exported (public API surface of package store), so every eventual caller is forced into that conflation; the name also implies a caller-supplied default, yet no default is accepted and none of the promised fallback semantics are implemented — the body simply returns the zero value. This is a present contract defect, not a future-caller speculation.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing and returns unambiguous empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported helper discards the error from Load (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`), so a missing key (Load returns "", ErrMissing) and a key that genuinely exists with an empty value (Load returns "", nil) both yield the same empty string with no error channel. Any caller cannot distinguish 'absent' from 'present-but-empty', and there is no parameter for a meaningful default — the fallback is forced to the zero value. Because this is a public API surface, the lossy contract ships now; the defect is the signature itself, not a hypothetical future caller.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load (src/store.go:7-13) returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when a key is present but holds an empty string. LoadOrDefault (src/store.go:15-18) discards the error and returns the bare string, so both cases collapse to "". Any caller cannot distinguish a missing key from a legitimately-empty stored value, and every eventual caller of this exported API is forced to conflate failure with a real value (e.g. reporting/persisting "" as a real config value). No in-repo caller exists yet, but the exported contract itself is the defect.

findings.title: Run returns before results are delivered; breaks completion/ordering contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `results <- j*2` ran synchronously in the loop, so `Run` blocked until every result had been handed to the channel (implicit happens-before + ordering). Now each send happens in a detached goroutine and `Run` returns immediately after launching them. The natural caller pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` now races the outstanding goroutines and panics with `send on closed channel`, and a caller that drains after `Run` returns can observe a partial or reordered result set. There is no WaitGroup or other completion signal, so callers cannot recover the old behavior.

findings.title: Unbounded goroutine fan-out with no cancellation or backpressure
findings.whyItBreaks: One goroutine is spawned per element of `jobs` with no worker-pool bound, and `ctx` is still never consulted. For a large `jobs` slice this is an unbounded concurrency/resource spike, and if the consumer stops receiving (or `ctx` is cancelled), every blocked sender on `results <- j*2` leaks for the lifetime of the process — after `Run` has already returned, so the caller has no way to wait for or reclaim them.

findings.title: Run no longer waits for results before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run sent each result into the caller's channel synchronously and only returned after all len(jobs) sends had completed, so a caller could rely on completion ordering (e.g. `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` or counting the exact number of received values). With the goroutine-per-job body, Run returns immediately and both the delivery and its ordering are unbounded in time relative to return: values may arrive after Run returns, out of order, or never if the caller stops consuming. Any caller that closes `results` after Run returns, or reuses/sizes state by len(jobs) once Run returns, now hits `send on closed channel` panic or silently lost results — a regression from the base behavior at src/worker.go:7-8.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; callers can panic or lose results
findings.whyItBreaks: Base sent every result synchronously, so when Run returned the results channel had received all len(jobs) values in job order. The change moves each send into a goroutine and never joins, so Run returns after launching work, not after completing it. Any caller using the idiomatic pattern of buffering results and closing after Run (e.g. `results := make(chan int, len(jobs)); Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)`) now races the still-running senders: a goroutine that has not yet sent hits `results <- j*2` on a closed channel and panics ('send on closed channel'), and callers that instead read exactly len(jobs) results then stop will leave the remaining sends blocked forever. In-repo callers/tests do not exist, but Run is exported, so this is the shipped contract of a public function.

findings.title: Log's new tag parameter is accepted but never used
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `func Log(message string, tag ...string)` (src/logger.go:3) advertises that callers can supply one or more tags, but the body only calls `println(message)` (src/logger.go:4) and never reads `tag`. Because `Log` is an exported/public symbol, the signature is the contract: any caller passing `Log("msg", "error")` receives output identical to `Log("msg")`, so the promised tag data is silently discarded. This is a public-carrier promise the body does not implement (the tag contents would be part of the emitted log a caller receives), which is a defect regardless of whether any in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: Log accepts `tag` parameter but never uses it
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `Log(message string, tag ...string)` advertises that callers can supply one or more tags, but the body only does `println(message)` and discards `tag` entirely. Any caller that passes a tag (e.g. `logger.Log("startup failed", "error")`) gets output with no trace of that tag and no error/return signal indicating the argument was dropped, so the caller cannot distinguish 'tag applied' from 'tag ignored'. The parameter is a no-op that changes nothing a caller observes, yet is presented as supported API.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now allows non-admins to delete tenant records
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate was `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`, so deletion required BOTH admin status AND a tenant match. Changing `&&` to `||` means a non-admin session whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId now evaluates to true, granting cross-user deletion of any record in the same tenant. The admin requirement is entirely bypassed; `record.ownerId` is never consulted, so a regular user can delete records they do not own. This is a live authorization bypass on an exported gate (`canDeleteRecord` is `export`ed), so every consumer inherits the widened permission regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord widened to OR allows unauthorized deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: Changed predicate `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` now returns true in two newly-authorized cases: (1) any non-admin whose tenantId matches the record is authorized to delete it, and (2) any admin is authorized to delete records in ANY tenant, breaking tenant isolation. Base behavior required BOTH admin and matching tenant. This function gates a destructive action (record deletion), so the widened predicate approves deletions that were previously denied — unauthorized data destruction / cross-tenant escalation.

findings.title: Authorization widening: admins can delete any tenant's records
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `&&` with `||` inverts the conjunctive authorization guard. The previous contract required BOTH `session.isAdmin` AND `session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. Now `session.isAdmin` alone short-circuits to `true`, so an admin of tenant A can delete records belonging to tenant B (cross-tenant privilege escalation). Symmetrically, any non-admin whose `tenantId` matches the record's now passes even without `isAdmin`, so a non-admin user of the same tenant gains delete rights they were previously denied. Both branches independently widen authorization, producing unauthorized deletes/data loss on a live permission path.

findings.title: clampPercent name promises clamping the body does not implement
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported symbol was renamed to `clampPercent`, but the body `Math.round((done / total) * 100)` performs no clamping to [0,100] and can return negative or >100 values (e.g. done=3,total=2 -> 150; done=-1,total=10 -> -10; total=0 -> Infinity). The one caller, `progressBar` (src/progress.ts:6-7), relies on the name's cap promise: it does `"#".repeat(pct) + "-".repeat(100 - pct)`, and for pct>100 (or pct<0) `String.repeat` receives a negative count and throws `RangeError: Invalid count value`, so `progressBar` can crash on out-of-range inputs the name claims are handled. Public/exported carrier, so the promise is the contract a caller trusts.

findings.title: Rename to clampPercent promises clamping the body never performs
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported symbol was renamed from `toPercent` to `clampPercent`, a name that promises a result clamped to [0,100]. The body (src/progress.ts:2) still returns the raw rounded ratio `Math.round((done/total)*100)` with no `Math.min`/`Math.max`, so `done > total` yields pct > 100 and `done < 0` yields a negative pct. Because the carrier is a PUBLIC export, the promise is the contract: callers trusting the clamp receive out-of-range values. The in-repo caller `progressBar` (src/progress.ts:7) relies on that bound — `"#".repeat(pct) + "-".repeat(100 - pct)` — and throws `RangeError: Invalid count value` once `100 - pct` goes negative (done > total). Renaming to a stronger promise while the body implements none of it is a contract drift, not an improvement.

findings.title: clampPercent never clamps; progressBar throws on out-of-range input
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name `clampPercent` promises a result constrained to [0, 100] (that is what "clamp" means), but the body still computes `Math.round((done / total) * 100)` with no lower/upper bound. Its own caller `progressBar` relies on that promise: it feeds `pct` into `"#".repeat(pct)` and `"-".repeat(100 - pct)`. With done > total, pct > 100 so `100 - pct` is negative and `"-".repeat(negative)` throws RangeError; with pct < 0 `"#".repeat` throws; with total === 0, pct is Infinity and repeat throws. A caller that substitutes the promised clamp behavior gets a crash instead of a clamped bar.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows invalid-input errors, resetting saved settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, parseSettings threw on malformed JSON or a non-string theme / non-number fontSize, so callers could detect and refuse the bad state. Now the catch-all returns { ...DEFAULTS }, making failure indistinguishable from a legitimate default-valued settings object. In-repo caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) then does `settings.fontSize = size; save(JSON.stringify(settings))`, so a corrupt or schema-drifted `raw` silently resets theme to "light" and writes that reset back through save(), discarding the user's persisted settings rather than surfacing the error. As an exported function, every external caller is likewise forced to conflate "invalid input" with "valid defaults".

findings.title: parseSettings swallows all failures and updateFontSize persists defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, parseSettings threw on malformed JSON or on a non-string theme / non-number fontSize, so parseSettings' caller saw a real error. The new `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS } }` maps every failure (JSON.parse error, 'bad theme', 'bad fontSize') to the DEFAULTS value with no signal. The in-repo caller updateFontSize @src/settings.ts:20-22 then mutates that fallback and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) @src/settings.ts:22. Concretely, if the stored raw is `{"theme":"dark"}` (missing fontSize) or otherwise fails validation, the previous code threw and never wrote; now it returns {theme:"light",fontSize:14}, sets fontSize=size, and overwrites the user's persisted settings with the default theme — silent loss of the user's theme (and any other fields) plus loss of the 'load failed' signal.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors, silently overwriting saved settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, malformed JSON or a missing/wrong-typed `theme`/`fontSize` threw out of parseSettings. The new catch-all maps every failure to `{ ...DEFAULTS }` with no log and no distinguishable marker, so callers can no longer tell "parse failed" from "legitimately default settings". The live in-repo caller `updateFontSize` (src/settings.ts:20-22) calls `parseSettings(raw)`, overwrites `fontSize`, and `save(JSON.stringify(settings))` — so on unparseable/partial persisted settings it now writes back `{theme:"light",fontSize:<size>}`, silently discarding the user's saved theme and clobbering the stored file with defaults. Previously that path threw and aborted the write, preserving the on-disk value.

findings.title: pageCount undercounts pages; last partial page unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount is the public contract for 'how many pages exist'. Math.floor discards the remainder, so totalItems=10, pageSize=3 returns 3 while 4 pages are required to cover all 10 items. Any caller sizing a page list, loop, or 'next page' bound from this value will drop the final partial page's items from view. Example: substitute totalItems=10, pageSize=3 -> Math.floor(10/3)=3 pages, but items 10..10 (the 4th page) become unreachable.

findings.title: Report pairs builtFrom commit with artifacts from wrong ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport now returns `{ builtFrom: commit, artifacts: build.artifactsAt(verified) }`, where `commit = build.ref(branch)` but `verified = build.ref("verified")`. The BuildReport contract (builtFrom/artifacts pair, src/report.ts:6-8) implies the returned artifacts belong to the reported commit. After this change the two fields are drawn from different refs: a caller asking for branch X gets `builtFrom` = X's commit while `artifacts` are whatever "verified" points at. The `branch` argument is now silently ignored for the artifacts half of the report, so any consumer that identifies or ships artifacts by the reported build commit will attribute/ship artifacts from the wrong revision. This is a wrong-output regression, not a style issue.

findings.title: buildReport attributes artifacts from hard-coded "verified" ref to branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, artifacts came from the same commit as builtFrom: `const commit = build.ref(branch); ... artifactsAt(commit)`. Now `artifacts` is fetched via `build.ref("verified")` (line 13) while `builtFrom` still reports `build.ref(branch)` (line 12). The two fields of the exported BuildReport now describe different revisions: a caller asking for branch B gets B's commit paired with whatever artifacts sit on the fixed "verified" ref, and the `branch` argument is silently ignored for artifact resolution. Because builtFrom and artifacts are returned together, any consumer that treats the artifact list as "the artifacts built from builtFrom" is misled whenever ref("verified") != ref(branch) (e.g. the branch is unreleased/unverified), where the old code returned the branch's own artifacts.

findings.title: Report artifacts no longer sourced from the reported builtFrom commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the artifacts were fetched with build.artifactsAt(commit) where commit = build.ref(branch), i.e. the same commit returned as builtFrom. The change introduces verified = build.ref("verified") and returns artifacts = build.artifactsAt(verified) while builtFrom still reports commit (the branch ref). The two fields of BuildReport are now derived from potentially different refs, so any consumer that correlates `builtFrom` with `artifacts` (e.g. shows "built from <commit>" alongside the artifact list, or diffs artifacts for a known commit) receives a self-inconsistent report and may attribute another ref's artifacts to the branch commit. If a `verified` ref is absent/empty the report silently lists artifacts for a wrong ref instead of failing, hiding the divergence.

findings.title: Restore limit cap in recentEntries (slice removed)
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaced `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` with a body that only handles `limit <= 0` and otherwise `return sorted`, dropping the cap entirely. The carrier `/** Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first. */` (src/feed.ts:1) still promises at most `limit` entries, but the body returns all `all.length` reversed entries whenever limit > 0. The only in-repo caller, renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9), passes limit=20 and relies on `page.length <= 20` when filling its fixed 20-element buffer (src/feed.ts:10-11): with all.length > 20, page.length exceeds 20, the loop writes `out[20..n]` which extends the array, and renderFeed returns more than its intended 20 entries. E.g. all.length=25, limit=20 → recentEntries returns 25 entries and renderFeed returns a length-25 array instead of a 20-entry page.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit`; returns unbounded list
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`, which honored the documented contract "Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first" @src/feed.ts:1. The new body reverses but never slices, so for any `limit > 0` it returns every element. Its only caller `renderFeed` @src/feed.ts:9 calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and sizes a page of 20 (`new Array<string>(20)` @src/feed.ts:10); with the dropped slice, `page.length` can exceed 20 and the loop @src/feed.ts:11 writes out[20], out[21]... growing the returned array to the full feed length. User-visible feed now returns more than the intended 20 entries (page size contract broken).

findings.title: recentEntries drops the limit cap and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new body builds `sorted` but returns it unsliced, so the `limit` argument is ignored for any limit > 0. The doc comment on line 1 still promises "at most `limit` entries". A caller passing a real cap now gets every entry: renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20) at src/feed.ts:9, then writes page into a 20-slot array at src/feed.ts:11; with page.length > 20 the loop extends `out` past 20, so renderFeed returns the entire reversed list instead of a 20-entry page — a user-facing regression in the feed output.

findings.title: entry-count header ignores stale filter, mismatching rendered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `live` filter drops stale entries from `rows` (line 21), but the header still receives the unfiltered `entries.length` (line 22). For any input containing stale entries, `# entry-count: N` reports the count of all entries while only `live.length` rows are written, so the declared entry count disagrees with the manifest contents it describes. Before this change the count equaled the row count (both `entries.length`); the diff introduces the divergence. Any consumer that sizes, paginates, or validates using the declared count against rendered rows will mis-read the manifest.

findings.title: entry-count header now counts stale rows that are not emitted
findings.whyItBreaks: The change filters `stale` entries out of `rows` (line 20-21) but the return still passes `entries.length` (line 22) to `headerLines`. The manifest now emits `# entry-count: <total>` while listing only the non-stale subset, so the count no longer matches the rows it labels. Any consumer that parses the manifest by reading `entry-count` and expecting that many row lines (or that uses the count for sizing/validation) will see a mismatch whenever any entry is stale — e.g. two entries where one is stale yields `# entry-count: 2` followed by a single row. Before this PR the count and rows were always consistent, so this is a regression introduced by the diff.

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches emitted rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters stale entries into `live` and renders only live rows, but line 22 still passes `entries.length` (the unfiltered total) to `headerLines`. The unchanged carrier `# entry-count: ${count}` (src/manifest.ts:15) promises the number of entries the manifest contains. Whenever at least one entry has `stale === true`, the header count exceeds the number of tab-separated data rows emitted. Any consumer that trusts `entry-count` to size/verify the manifest (reading exactly N rows, asserting completeness, or allocating for N entries) now reads a count that disagrees with the body, yielding a wrong count or a failed parse. The base version was consistent because rows and count were both derived from `entries`.

findings.title: execute() always throws instead of returning input
findings.whyItBreaks: The body was changed from `return input.toUpperCase();` to `throw new Error("always fails");`. The declared contract is `(input: string): string`, so every call now raises an uncaught exception and no caller can ever receive a string. This converts a working transformation into a hard failure on the only exported code path; the string parameter is also no longer used for anything.

findings.title: Restore return value; execute() now throws on every call
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `execute(input: string): string` previously returned `input.toUpperCase()` and now unconditionally executes `throw new Error("always fails")`. Every caller of this public function gets an exception instead of the string its signature still promises, so the function is unusable on all inputs — a hard regression of the module's only exported behavior.

findings.title: execute() now throws unconditionally, breaking its string contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change execute(input) returned input.toUpperCase(), a value satisfying the declared `: string` return type. Now the body unconditionally executes `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every call throws and no code path can ever produce a return value. The exported function is the sole entry point of the module; any caller that previously relied on the returned uppercased string now fails at runtime with an error instead of receiving a value, and the thrown error carries no actionable information. This is not a narrowed guard or an added error branch — it removes the only success path.

findings.title: New viewer guard over-blocks eligible viewers, breaking read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false for req.role==="viewer" before the attempts check. handle() at line 24 calls isEligible first and returns "rejected" when it is false, so the viewer branch at line 25 (`if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";`) is now dead code. Concretely, an active viewer with attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS returned "read-only" at base (d930eda) but returns "rejected" at head (81ebab4) — a real behavior change on a live path. Viewers are a legitimate entitlement the eligibility predicate should not govern; the viewer-specific handling already lives downstream in handle().

findings.title: isEligible viewer rejection makes handle()'s read-only path unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER A over-block. Before this change, handle() served active viewers: isEligible returned true (status active, attempts < 5), so the guard at line 25 returned "read-only". The new predicate line 18 (`if (req.role === "viewer") return false;`) makes isEligible reject every viewer, so handle() now hits line 24 and returns "rejected" first. Line 25 `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` is now unreachable dead code. isEligible gates general request routing, not role authorization; role-specific handling is meant to happen downstream in handle(), so the tightened predicate over-blocks a legitimately-servable viewer action. Concrete: req={status:"active",role:"viewer",attempts:0} previously produced "read-only", now produces "rejected". The line-19 refactor to tooMany(attempts) is behavior-preserving (attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS unchanged); only the role clause is the regression.

findings.title: Viewer gate makes handle()'s read-only branch unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible() now returns false for req.role==="viewer", but the only caller of isEligible() is handle(), which already handles viewers as a legitimate distinct outcome: `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` (src/handler.ts:25). After this change that branch can never execute, so an active viewer with attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS that previously returned "read-only" now returns "rejected" at src/handler.ts:24. The author's own intent is contradicted by the newly-dead line 25.

findings.title: Payment gate wrongly blocks saveDraft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by both submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). The change adds `&& order.payment === "paid"` to the shared gate, so saveDraft now returns "blocked" for any draft whose payment is still "missing". Saving a draft is a legitimately approvable action that does not depend on payment; a draft is by definition pre-payment. Before this diff, canProceed({state:"draft",payment:"missing"}) was true and saveDraft returned "saved"; now it is false and saveDraft returns "blocked". Payment validity is only a legitimate precondition for submission, so adding it to the shared predicate over-blocks the save-draft workflow.

findings.title: canProceed payment gate wrongly blocks saveDraft for unpaid orders
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by two distinct actions. Adding `order.payment === "paid"` correctly tightens submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4), but saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) legitimately saves a draft regardless of payment. With payment === "missing", canProceed now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved" for a draft order — rejecting an action that is approvable independent of this gate's concern.

findings.title: saveDraft blocked for unpaid drafts by shared canProceed gate
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now returns order.state !== "ready" && order.payment === "paid". saveDraft shares this predicate, so an order with state "draft" and payment "missing" yields canProceed=false and returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Saving a draft is a pre-submission action that is legitimately approvable without payment — the shared predicate should not govern it. (submitOrder legitimately needs payment, so the requirement is correct only for that call-site.)

findings.title: Snapshot files no longer match reported commit/channel
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot resolved `head = repo.headCommit(channel)` and returns it as `commit` together with the passed `channel`, but the changed line 18 now reads `files: repo.filesAt(stable)`, where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` (line 14). The returned `files` list is now the file set of the "stable" ref regardless of which channel was requested, so a published snapshot claims channel X/commit X while shipping stable's contents — a wrong-data/wrong-route outcome for every caller (including any channel other than "stable" and any caller publishing a feature channel).

findings.title: publishSnapshot reports channel commit but files from stable
findings.whyItBreaks: head = repo.headCommit(channel) is still stored as Snapshot.commit, but files is now repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). The snapshot contract promises a commit and the files at that commit; consumers will publish/record the stable branch's file contents under the channel's commit SHA. Every snapshot is internally inconsistent (files do not exist at the reported commit unless the two refs coincide), which silently corrupts whatever is keyed by snapshot.commit. Additionally, 'stable' is a hard-coded ref that may not exist for repos using this interface, so headCommit("stable") can fail where headCommit(channel) previously succeeded.

findings.title: Snapshot reports channel head commit but files from "stable"
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot() still sets `commit` to `repo.headCommit(channel)` (src/publish.ts:13) but now computes `files` from `repo.filesAt(stable)` where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` (src/publish.ts:14,18). The returned Snapshot is internally inconsistent: the reported commit does not correspond to the returned file list. For any channel whose head differs from "stable" (e.g. the default "main"), consumers receive the file listing of a different commit than the one they are told was published, so the snapshot content is silently wrong. This is a behavioral regression versus the prior code, which used `repo.filesAt(head)`.

findings.title: `limit` parameter is ignored; output always capped at 10
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature now advertises `build(prefix, limit=10)` (src/builder.py:1), which promises the caller can cap the result size, but the body still hardcodes `max_count = 10` (src/builder.py:2) and iterates `range(max_count)` (src/builder.py:4). `limit` is referenced nowhere else in the file, so `build("p", limit=3)` returns 10 elements instead of 3 — the caller's cap is silently dropped and the returned data is larger than requested.

findings.title: Unused `limit` parameter makes build() promise a cap it ignores
findings.whyItBreaks: `build` gains a public `limit=10` parameter, but the body still hardcodes `max_count = 10` (src/builder.py:2) and the loop range is driven by `max_count`, so `limit` is dead. Any caller passing `build("x", limit=3)` still receives 10 items and any caller passing `limit=100` still receives 10. The signature advertises result capping/filtering that the body does not perform, forcing every caller to conflate the requested cap with the actual (fixed) output size.

findings.title: build() ignores new limit arg; hardcoded cap contradicts signature
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature `def build(prefix, limit=10)` promises the returned list is capped/bounded by the caller-supplied `limit`, but the body never reads `limit` and instead computes `max_count = 10` at src/builder.py:2, running `for i in range(max_count)` at src/builder.py:4. Any caller passing `limit=3` still receives 10 elements, so the promised cap is silently not applied — a public carrier whose promise the body does not implement.

findings.title: `parse_positive_int` does not validate positivity
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename from `read_int` to `parse_positive_int` makes the function name a public contract that the returned value is validated as a positive integer, but the body is still just `int(value)`, which accepts negative and zero values (e.g. `parse_positive_int(-5)` returns `-5`, `parse_positive_int(0)` returns `0`). Any caller that trusts the name and skips its own check passes these values straight through: `charge(amount)` @src/validators.py:5-7 computes `n * 100`, so a negative amount yields a negative charge, and `total_cents` @src/validators.py:10-11 sums them into a negative "total". The promised validation is absent, so failure/limiting behavior the name advertises silently does not happen.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises validation it never performs
findings.whyItBreaks: The symbol now advertises 'positive' validation (Trigger C contract carrier: the public name is the contract), but the body is a bare int(value) with no positivity check. A caller passing a negative or zero value gets no rejection: parse_positive_int(-5) returns -5, and charge(-5) returns -500, silently propagating a bogus negative charge. Callers naming this function will trust the positivity guarantee rather than re-validating.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but never validates it
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename advertises a validated contract ('positive int'), but the body is unchanged `return int(value)`. `int()` accepts negatives and zero (e.g. parse_positive_int(-5) == -5, parse_positive_int(0) == 0) and never raises on non-positive input. Its only in-repo caller, `charge` at src/validators.py:6, trusts the name and multiplies the result: charge(-5) returns -500, and `total_cents` (src/validators.py:11) then propagates a negative total. Any caller relying on the name skips its own positivity guard, so invalid amounts are silently accepted and produce negative money values instead of failing.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates the caller's DataFrame in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `result = df.copy()` made apply_values side-effect free: it returned a new frame and left the input untouched. The new body writes directly into the argument (`df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value`) and returns the same object, so every caller's input frame is silently mutated. Because both the return value and the argument now alias the same object, callers that kept the original `df` for later steps (comparison, aggregation, export, or a second apply_values pass) will observe values they never intended to change. This is an input-aliasing regression introduced by this PR, not style.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame in place

The diff drops the copy and writes directly into the parameter (`df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value`) and returns that same object. Any caller that reuses the passed-in DataFrame after calling apply_values now observes mutated rows/values; the function silently gained a destructive side effect on caller-owned state. With no callers in-repo the public contract is still broken: the mutation is observable to every eventual caller, and callers that assumed non-mutation (e.g., passing the same frame to two different mappings, or holding a reference for later comparison) will get wrong results.

findings.title: apply_values mutates caller's DataFrame instead of returning a copy
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version did `result = df.copy()` and applied mapping to the copy, so callers could keep using their original df unchanged. The head version drops the copy, writes through `df.loc[...] = value` directly onto the caller's object, and returns that same object. Any caller that holds or uses its `df` after calling (e.g. `apply_values(df, mapping); ...df...`) now sees its `"value"` column silently overwritten. The function's non-mutating contract changed with no signal to callers; the diff offers no doc, rename, or version bump to alert them.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but never validates it
findings.whyItBreaks: The public symbol was renamed read_int -> parse_positive_int, so its name now promises a validated, positive result. The body is unchanged: `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` only parses and silently defaults to 0 on failure. It performs no positivity check, so negative inputs flow through. The public caller `charge` @src/parse.rs:6 (unchanged) multiplies the value by 100, so `charge("-5")` returns -500 and `charge("abc")` returns 0 — both violate the promised "positive" contract, and a negative charge is exactly what the name says cannot happen. Because parse_positive_int is `pub`, the name is the API contract, and any consumer reading the label to assume a positive, validated amount gets a value the implementation does not guarantee.

The caller `charge` (line 6) trusts the positive guarantee and returns `n * 100`, so a negative or garbage amount silently yields a negative or zero charge (e.g. "-5" -> -500, "abc" -> 0) instead of erroring, which a caller relying on the name would never expect.

findings.title: Remove leftover dbg! that dumps caller data to stderr
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `dbg!(items)` is a leftover debugging artifact that executes on every call, unconditionally writing `[src/store.rs:2] items = [...]` plus the full Debug rendering of the caller's `items` vector to stderr. This is a new side effect not present at the base revision: it leaks whatever the caller passes (potentially PII, tokens, or user content) into process stderr/logs, and floods logs with unbounded, attacker-influenced output. findings.title: dbg!(items) moves the Vec, breaking compilation of process
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, which takes its argument by value. `items: Vec<String>` is not `Copy`, so `dbg!(items);` on line 2 moves `items` into the match temporary (dropped at the end of the statement). The unchanged line 3 `let total = items.len();` then uses the moved value, producing a hard compile error (`error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `items``) — the crate cannot build. Additionally, this leftover debug macro unconditionally dumps the full contents of every `items` argument to stderr, leaking caller data into logs even if the move were fixed (e.g. by `dbg!(&items)`).

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items, breaking the following items.len()
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!($val)` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!("... {:#?}", &tmp); tmp } }`. Matching on `items` with the by-value binding `tmp` moves the `Vec<String>` into `tmp`; the arm value is discarded at the statement's semicolon, so `items` is moved and dropped. The next line `let total = items.len();` (src/store.rs:3) then reuses the moved value and fails to compile with E0382 'use of moved value: items'. The public `process` function therefore cannot build at all, and the crate loses any usable path through it. (If the macro were fixed to compile, it would additionally dump the caller's item contents to stderr.)

findings.title: changedPaths computed against latest but reported as fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract (src/changeset.ts:7-9) states fromRevision is "Revision the changed paths were computed against" and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly that revision. The new line 15 resolves 'latest' and line 18 computes changedPaths via store.readChangedPaths(latest), while line 17 still emits fromRevision from store.resolve(pinnedTag). When pinnedTag != latest these two fields describe different base revisions: a consumer replaying the returned paths on top of fromRevision applies paths computed against a different revision, yielding an incorrect changeset (changes between pinnedTag and latest are dropped or changes already contained in fromRevision are re-applied). Even in the single-revision case readChangedPaths(latest) describes the delta from latest, not from the pinned tag the function is documented and named around.

findings.title: changedPaths no longer computed against reported fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The public interface documents that fromRevision is 'Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' Before the diff, changedPaths was derived from `from` (the pinned tag), so the two fields were a consistent pair. After the change, changedPaths is derived from a second, independent `store.resolve("latest")` value while fromRevision remains `from`. Every consumer that replays changedPaths on top of fromRevision is now using a changeset whose base does not match the base the paths were produced from: if readChangedPaths(r) returns the changes relative to r, the listed paths are those since `latest` rather than since the pinned revision (dropping/altering the intended change set), and if it returns a single revision's own paths, it returns latest's paths instead of the pinned revision's. Either way the exported carrier's promise is false and consumers receive an inconsistent fromRevision/changedPaths pair.

findings.title: changedPaths no longer relative to fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The unchanged Changeset contract at src/changeset.ts:7-8 states fromRevision is 'the revision the changed paths were computed against' and that consumers 'replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' This diff computes changedPaths from store.resolve("latest") (line 15/18) while still reporting fromRevision = store.resolve(pinnedTag) (line 17). The returned object is now internally inconsistent: paths are a diff from the latest revision but are labeled as a diff from the pinned revision, so any consumer that replays changedPaths on top of fromRevision applies the wrong delta to the wrong base. The carrier (the doc comment and the exported field pairing) is public, so the promise is the contract even absent in-repo callers.

findings.title: Inverted authz check lets non-admins purge projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The base predicate purged only when `user.isAdmin && project.archived`. This is an authorization inversion: an unprivileged user can trigger a destructive delete (data loss / authz bypass), and simultaneously a legitimate admin can never purge (the action becomes forbidden even when it should be approvable). findings.title: Charge swallows submit error and returns nil on failed payment
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code returned `fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` when gw.Submit failed, letting callers detect and handle a declined/failed charge. The new code only logs the error and falls through to `return nil`, so Charge now signals success for a charge that never completed. Every caller (this is an exported package function, so the error contract is the API promise) will treat a failed charge as paid — e.g. marking an order paid, persisting state, or releasing goods without money captured. Failure is no longer distinguishable from a legitimate success value.

findings.title: Charge swallows Submit error and reports success

Now, on any `gw.Submit` error the function only logs and falls through to `return nil`, so the exported public contract (`func Charge(...) error`) reports success for a payment that never happened. Any caller that branches on the returned error (e.g. to mark an order paid, grant access, or record a billing event) can no longer distinguish "charged" from "gateway declined/succeeded=false/transport error", and will treat the failure as a real successful charge — a silent failure-as-value path that can cause fulfillment without payment or missed reconciliation.

findings.title: Charge swallows gateway error and returns nil on failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously a failed gw.Submit returned `charge failed: %w` to the caller. Now the error is only logged and the function falls through to `return nil`. Charge is an exported (public) API whose sole failure signal is its error return; every caller that inspects the returned error will see success for a payment that actually failed, then proceed to persist, fulfill, or bill on a charge that never happened. Logging is not a substitute for the returned signal because no caller can observe the log to distinguish failure from success.

findings.title: Save silently drops file Close error, reporting failures as success
findings.whyItBreaks: The base revision returned `f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24), so any error surfaced while closing the file — the point where the OS may still fail a deferred flush (e.g. ENOSPC/NFS/fsync-on-close) — propagated to the caller. A caller that sees `nil` now cannot distinguish a durable write from a close/flush failure, so a persisted write may be treated as successful. findings.title: Save discards f.Close() error, hiding failed writes

With the error discarded, `Save` returns nil even though the data was not durably written, so an exported function's caller cannot distinguish success from a failed write and may treat unpersisted data as saved. findings.title: Fix inverted TTL check returning expired cache values
findings.whyItBreaks: The TTL predicate was flipped from `< this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`. `get` now returns `entry.value` only when the entry's age EXCEEDS the TTL (i.e. it is expired) and falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null` when the entry is still fresh. Result: `TtlCache` serves stale/expired data and treats every live entry as a miss, negating the cache's freshness contract and returning stale values to any caller (auth/session/rate-limit style consumers read stale state).

findings.title: Fix pruneDone skipping adjacent done jobs via forward splice
findings.whyItBreaks: `forEach` iterates forward while `jobs.splice(index, 1)` removes the current element, shifting all later elements down one index. The next iteration advances to index+1, skipping the element that moved into the vacated slot. For input `[{done:true},{done:true}]`, index 0 is spliced and index 1 is skipped, so a done job survives pruning. `pruneDone`'s name/contract promises removal of all done jobs; the body fails to deliver, and any caller relying on the returned list being done-free gets stale entries back.

findings.title: Avoid mutating caller's array in pruneDone

findings.title: Restore TTL check: cache now returns expired values and misses fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped to `Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs`. With `>`, `get` returns `entry.value` only when the entry has EXCEEDED its TTL (stale), and for a fresh entry (`elapsed <= ttlMs`) it takes the else branch, deletes the key, and returns null. This inverts the TTL contract: callers receive expired data as if valid and treat every fresh entry as a cache miss (so it is also evicted). The base version used `<`, which correctly returned the value while still fresh.

findings.title: Fix splice-while-iterating: adjacent done jobs are not pruned

Example: `pruneDone([{done:true},{done:true}])` returns `[{done:true}]` — one done job survives; with all-done input roughly every other element leaks. Additionally, the previous `filter` returned a NEW array and left the caller's array untouched, whereas the new body mutates the caller's array in place and returns the same reference, changing existing callers' input.

findings.title: TtlCache.get inverts TTL check, serving expired values and dropping fresh ones

Now an entry whose age EXCEEDS the TTL (expired) is returned as `entry.value`, while a fresh entry (age < ttlMs) falls through to `this.entries.delete(key)` and returns null. On every get the cache hands stale data to callers and evicts valid entries, so a TtlCache never serves a fresh hit and never rejects a stale one.

findings.title: pruneDone skips adjacent done jobs and mutates the caller's array

After removing index i, the element that moves into index i is never visited, so consecutive done jobs are dropped from pruning. With input `[{done:true},{done:true}]` the result is `[{done:true}]` instead of `[]`, i.e. a done job survives and can be reprocessed. It also now mutates the caller's array in place and returns the same reference, whereas the previous `filter` returned a new array and left the input untouched.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN on empty rows after guard removal

findings.title: Restore numeric score sort; default sort() ranks lexicographically

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator converts each number to a string and compares UTF-16 code units, so the ranking is lexicographic, not numeric. topPlayers derives its cutoff from the 1-indexed element at n of that ordering (line 15) and then filters with p.score >= cutoff (line 16). findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: The change swaps `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` for `expected == given_signature`. Python's `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the runtime of the comparison depends on how many leading characters of the attacker-supplied `given_signature` match the expected digest. An attacker who can submit many webhook requests and measure response timing can recover the expected HMAC-SHA256 digest byte-by-byte and forge valid signatures, bypassing the 401 gate in `handle()` (app/webhook.py:14). The module still imports `hmac` (line 2) and `signature_of` returns a hexdigest, i.e. the value being compared is a secret-derived MAC — exactly the case `compare_digest` exists to protect.

findings.title: Restore hmac.compare_digest in signature verification
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() previously compared the computed HMAC against the caller-supplied signature with hmac.compare_digest, which is constant-time. The change to `==` makes the comparison short-circuit on the first differing byte, so an attacker can recover a valid signature one byte at a time from response timing. verify() gates the 401/200 decision and execution of `processor(payload)` in handle() (app/webhook.py:14-16), so a forged signature that passes this check lets an unauthenticated caller drive arbitrary payload processing — a security bypass on a live path.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() now compares the expected HMAC against the attacker-supplied signature with '==', which short-circuits on the first differing byte. The prior implementation used hmac.compare_digest, which is constant-time. Because verify() gates authentication in handle() (app/webhook.py:14), a remote caller can measure comparison timing over many requests to recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and forge webhook payloads, bypassing the check entirely.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs executed inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. The refactor only wraps `_record_ledger` in the transaction and calls `_apply_balances(db, from_acct, to_acct, cents)` on line 24 after the transaction has committed. If `_apply_balances` fails (e.g. the debit UPDATE succeeds but the credit UPDATE raises, or the process dies between them), the ledger already shows the transfer as committed while the account balances are unchanged or only debited — a permanent ledger/balance desync (money silently lost or created). Even in autocommit mode the two UPDATEs are no longer atomic with each other or with the ledger row.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base revision all three writes (ledger INSERT + both balance UPDATEs) ran inside `with db.transaction():`, so the transfer was atomic. After the change, only `_record_ledger` (line 23) runs in the transaction and commits; `_apply_balances` (line 24) runs afterward, outside any transaction. If `_apply_balances` raises (missing account, constraint violation, connection loss, 2nd UPDATE failing after the 1st) or the process dies at line 24, the committed ledger row survives while balances are never updated (or only debited/credited). The ledger then records a transfer that did not happen, and the two balance mutations are no longer atomic with each other, so funds can be created or destroyed. The function still returns {"ok": True} on success and there is no compensating rollback.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version the ledger INSERT and both UPDATE accounts statements ran together inside `with db.transaction():`, so the whole transfer committed or rolled back as a unit. The PR now commits only `_record_ledger` inside the transaction (line 23) and executes `_apply_balances` (lines 8-16) afterward at line 24, outside any transaction. If the process crashes or `_apply_balances` raises after the ledger commit, the ledger row is persisted while balances are never adjusted. If the second UPDATE fails (e.g. destination account missing) the debit has already been applied/committed and the credit is lost. In all these cases recorded ledger and actual balances diverge — money is created or destroyed — with no way to recover atomically.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local-time getters instead of UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body used at.getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new body uses at.getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which resolve the calendar day in the runtime's local timezone. The exported contract (billingDay / sameBillingDay) is a day key, and the prior UTC basis made it deterministic. Substituting a real value: at = new Date('2026-03-01T02:00:00Z') -> old returns '2026-03-01' (UTC) but new returns '2026-02-28' under America/Los_Angeles (UTC-8), so a charge at 02:00Z is attributed to the previous day. Conversely new Date('2026-03-01T00:30:00+09:00') has the same local (Tokyo) day but a different UTC day, so sameBillingDay(a,b) at src/billing/day.ts:8 now returns a host-dependent result for identical inputs. Because the runtime timezone is not controlled here, the same timestamp yields different billing days on different hosts/clients.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, not UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned a UTC calendar day via getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which resolve in the runtime's local timezone. The same instant therefore yields different billing days depending on the host/process TZ and on DST, so day-boundary instants get misclassified (e.g. 2024-01-01T02:00:00Z is '2024-01-01' in UTC but '2023-12-31' under TZ=America/Los_Angeles). For a billing-day key this is a determinism regression that can double-bill or skip a billing day on boundaries, and sameBillingDay inherits it.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time instead of UTC (TZ-dependent result)

Example: 2026-03-01T00:30:00Z yields "2026-03-01" under TZ=UTC (old and CI behavior) but "2026-02-28" under TZ=America/Los_Angeles (new). findings.title: Throw from retryBackground on exhausted attempts, not return void
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported retryBackground catches every thrown error and `continue`s; when the last attempt fails the loop ends and the function falls off the end returning void (line 30), which is byte-for-byte identical to a successful run. The failure is never logged, rethrown, or encoded in a return value, so a caller cannot distinguish 'all attempts failed' from 'succeeded' and will proceed/report/persist as though the operation worked (TRIGGER D — public swallow site: the unusable void contract is shipping now, independent of in-repo callers).

findings.title: retryBackground discards the failure signal of exhausted retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The added exported retryBackground returns void on every path: the catch block at lines 27-29 swallows the thrown error and `continue`s, and after the loop is exhausted the function falls off the end (line 30-31) with no throw/return value. Every caller is therefore forced to treat 'fn never succeeded' as 'fn succeeded', so a caller that persists/bills/reports on return will record a phantom success. This is a public API, so the unusable contract is a present defect even though no in-repo caller exists.

findings.title: Config rename timeoutMs->timeout silently disables the deadline guard

Existing consumers that still pass `{ timeoutMs: N }` now produce `config.timeout === undefined`, so `const deadline = Date.now() + config.timeout` (lines 8 and 21) becomes `NaN`; the guards `Date.now() > deadline` (lines 10 and 23) then evaluate to `false` forever, so the timeout protection silently stops working instead of failing loudly. findings.title: Renaming exported Config.timeoutMs to timeout silently disables the deadline guard

A consumer built from JSON/plain JS that still passes `{maxAttempts, timeoutMs}` yields config.timeout === undefined, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined` is NaN (@src/retry.ts:8) and the guard `if (Date.now() > deadline) return;` @src/retry.ts:10 is always false (NaN comparison), i.e. the timeout no longer bounds attempts. findings.title: Field reads .length on string|number, breaking numeric values
findings.whyItBreaks: The interface now declares `value: string | number` (line 2), so callers may legitimately pass a number, but line 6 computes `value.length`. Numbers have no `length`, so the template string evaluates to `len=undefined`; TypeScript also rejects `.length` on the `number` arm of the widened union, failing a strict build/typecheck.

findings.title: Input defaultValue no longer renders the field value

findings.title: Field.value admits number but body reads value.length

Substitution: value=5 → (5).length === undefined → label="len=undefined" → input defaultValue="len=undefined" (wrong rendered output). It is also a type error (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'`) under any TS build, so the widened contract is not implemented by the body.

findings.title: Field input no longer renders its value, only a length label

findings.title: value.length on widened `string | number` yields 'len=undefined'
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff widens FieldProps.value to `string | number` (line 2), but line 6 reads `value.length`. A JS number has no `.length`, so `value.length` is `undefined`; for any number passed (now a legal prop per the exported interface), label becomes the literal `len=undefined`.
