findings.title: Deploy workflow echoes the TOKEN secret into build logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step materializes ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} in the environment and then prints it via `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. GitHub's log masking is best-effort only and is bypassed by any transformation of the value (substring/slicing/encoding/`jq`/set -x tracing), so a deploy credential can be written into workflow run logs that are readable by anyone with repo/ Actions access and are retained for the run's lifetime. Because the workflow triggers on `on: push` for every branch, any pushed commit (including from a compromised contributor account with push rights) runs this and can exfiltrate the token. The step serves no functional purpose (the value is only printed, never consumed by `make build`), so the exposure is pure downside.

findings.title: Stop echoing the TOKEN secret into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step exports `secrets.TOKEN` into the environment and runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, printing the secret to the Actions run log. Log masking in GitHub Actions is best-effort (only exact-string matches are redacted, and any transformation, substring split, or quoting change defeats it), so the credential can land in run logs that are readable by anyone with repo read access and retained per log retention. Nothing in the step consumes the token for a real purpose, so the only effect of the added lines is exposure.

findings.title: Stop echoing secret TOKEN into deploy workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step exports secrets.TOKEN into the job environment and then runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the credential to the workflow log. GitHub log masking is best-effort (it fails for values that aren't registered secrets, for multi-line/encoded values, and for any downstream consumer that scrapes raw logs), so this turns a repository secret into a durable cleartext credential reachable by anyone with Actions log read access. Because the workflow triggers on every `push`, the secret is re-exposed on each push (including from branches), maximizing blast radius.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() or large diffs crash the adapter
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is the helper that materializes the full patch via git(['diff', mergeBase, headSha], cwd) at line 140. Removing maxBuffer drops spawnSync to Node's default stdout cap of 1 MiB; when the diff exceeds it, spawnSync sets res.error (ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER) and res.status === null, so line 38 throws 'git diff ... failed:'. That call site is outside the try/catch that begins at line 176, so the whole runGithub rejects with no result and no check-run posted, instead of the intended 'review failed' fallback. The sibling helpers gh() (line 16) and ghText() (line 27) still pass maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64, so this change is inconsistent and unintentional-looking for exactly the largest output in the adapter.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() so large PR diffs don't fail
findings.whyItBreaks: git() now runs spawnSync with Node's default maxBuffer (1 MiB). The unsized call is `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` at line 140, which returns the entire PR patch. Any patch over 1 MiB (large PRs, lockfiles, generated files) overflows the buffer: spawnSync sets res.error to ENOBUFS and res.status to null, so the `res.status !== 0` check at line 38 throws with empty stderr. Line 140 runs before the try at line 176, so the throw escapes runGithub (no review posted, no failure check-run written) and the CI run breaks for exactly the PRs this tool targets.

findings.title: Restore git maxBuffer or large PR diffs crash the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The `git` helper previously set maxBuffer to 64 MiB; the change drops it, so spawnSync uses Node's default 1 MiB stdout cap. `runGithub` pipes the full `git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>` patch through this helper (src/adapters/github.ts:140). For any PR whose patch exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated code, vendored deps), spawnSync kills the child and sets result.error=ENOBUFS with status=null; `res.status !== 0` is then true, so the helper throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty stderr. That throw happens at line 140, before the try block (line 176), so no check-run is posted and the CI step fails outright. Sibling `gh` helpers (lines 19 and 29) still keep `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64`, showing the cap was intentional and its loss here is accidental. Rows exceeding the cap would otherwise be silently truncated into an incomplete patch, which is also wrong.

findings.title: Restore the forced read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `-s read-only` was the only thing pinning the delegated `codex exec` process to a read-only sandbox. Without it, sandbox mode falls back to CLI config: with no `sandbox_mode` set, codex's config resolver (codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs:826-836) selects `WorkspaceWrite` whenever the active project directory has any trust decision (`active_project.filter(|p| p.is_trusted() || p.is_untrusted()).map(|_| SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite)`), and `read-only` only applies when a project is untrusted or config explicitly says so. This environment's `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` sets `trust_level = "trusted"` for this repo, so `runCodex` now spawns codex with a writable working tree (cwd = opts.repoPath). The prompt passed via stdin carries untrusted diff/PR content, so prompt-injection can now cause model-generated shell commands to modify or delete files in the repo under review (or any writable root), where previously writes were blocked outright. This is not cosmetic: the read-only guarantee is exactly what makes running an LLM over untrusted input safe.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox on codex exec in runCodex
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` means the sandbox is no longer pinned; codex resolves it from config. In this runner's environment (managed CODEX_HOME marks the reviewed checkout `[projects."..."].trust_level = "trusted"`) codex 0.159.3 resolves `sandbox_mode` to `workspace-write` — verified via `codex debug prompt-input`, which reports: "`sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`". Since spawnSync runs codex with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, the model (fed the attacker-controlled diff/prompt on stdin, approvals never prompted in exec mode) can now create/modify/delete files inside the repository under review and under /tmp, defeating the review agent's read-only guarantee.

findings.title: Restore pinned read-only sandbox on nested codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex feeds untrusted PR/repo content into a nested `codex exec` agent and previously pinned the sandbox with `-s read-only`, guaranteeing model-generated shell commands could not write or execute. Removing the flag delegates the sandbox to codex's ambient resolution: `sandbox_mode` / `default_permissions` / profiles in `~/.codex/config.toml` and `-c` overrides. Any user whose config loosens this for interactive use (e.g. `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or a `project-edit`/`danger-full-access` profile) now gets a nested agent, driven by possibly malicious diff text, executing commands and writing files in the reviewed workspace — a capability `-s read-only` made impossible.

findings.title: Diff against merge-base and posted headSha, not baseSha/HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, the patch was `git diff merge-base(baseSha, headSha) headSha` (three-dot-equivalent), so only the PR's own commits were reviewed (`mergeBase` @138 deleted). Now `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff against the base-branch SHA. When baseSha is the PR base tip from the workflow (base has advanced past the fork) it is not an ancestor of HEAD, so the diff additionally contains the reverse of every base-only commit the PR branch lacks — hunks the author never wrote, and base commits rendered as deletions. The head side was also changed from the computed `headSha` (which may come from PR_HEAD_SHA @137 and is the commit used for posting, `postReview` @178 / `postCheck` @179 and `Bundle.headSha` @165) to the literal local `HEAD`; if PR_HEAD_SHA != local HEAD, the reviewed patch is a different commit than the one comments/checks are posted to, so inline-comment line numbers (side RIGHT @66) can be rejected or attach to wrong lines.

findings.title: Diff now uses baseSha..HEAD, dropping merge-base and PR head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR's changes are no longer computed as merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha. `git diff baseSha HEAD` diffs the raw base SHA against whatever commit is checked out. On the standard GitHub Actions pull_request checkout, HEAD is the synthetic merge commit (refs/pull/N/merge = base tip merged with the PR head), so the patch and changedFileSet include base-branch content/conflict resolutions that are not in the PR head, and the hunks are rendered against the newer base rather than the PR's fork point. changedPaths (line 141) is then built from this wider set, so inlineComments (github.ts:61-70) can target files/lines that are not part of the PR, while the review is still posted with commit_id = headSha (github.ts:178) — the reviewed diff no longer corresponds to the revision under review, and GitHub inline-comment positions can be rejected or misplaced. If the workflow checks out the PR head branch instead of the merge ref, diffing the advanced base tip against the forked head additionally renders already-merged base-branch commits as spurious reversions. Both regressions disappear only when PR_* env vars are unset (HEAD==headSha), which is not the 'must run in Actions' path the function targets.

findings.title: Restore merge-base diff; two-dot baseSha..HEAD pulls in unrelated base changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line `git merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` existed because baseSha is not guaranteed to equal the PR fork point (its fallback is merge-base origin/main HEAD, but PR_BASE_SHA is a caller-supplied base ref/tip). `git diff baseSha HEAD` (and `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` inside changedFileSet) is a two-dot diff, so whenever the base branch has commits absent from HEAD it emits those commits in reverse as extra hunks and lists their files as changed. The bundle.patch then contains changes the PR never authored, changedFiles/changedPaths are over-inclusive, and a model finding anchored to such an unrelated path can make postReview's inline-comment payload reference a path outside the PR diff (GitHub 422), silently degrading to the catch-all fallback review. Additionally the right side is now the literal `HEAD` rather than `headSha`, so when PR_HEAD_SHA differs from HEAD the patch no longer corresponds to the headSha the bundle/review/check-run advertise.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so bundle/patch text is inserted literally
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement interprets $-patterns from the replacement text: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` token, `` $` ``→everything before the match, `$'`→everything after it. The substituted content is JSON.stringify(bundle) / JSON.stringify(candidate) / bundle.patch — i.e. raw diff and prompt text — so a diff containing `$&` or a bash `$'...'`/`$$` (very common in shell, sed/awk, node/perl replacement code) silently rewrites the prompt: e.g. `{"patch": "... $' ..."}` injects the entire tail of review.md/critic.md after the placeholder instead of the patch, and a literal `$$` debases to `$`. The base revision passed `() => JSON.stringify(...)` / `() => bundle.patch`, which inserts the value verbatim; this PR removes that protection (same defect on lines 32 and 33). Verified: node -e 'JSON.stringify("T {{B}} T2".replace("{{B}}", () => "[$& $`x $\' $1 $$]"))' ⇒ "T [$& $`x $' $1 $$] T2" (literal), while the string form yields "T [{{B}} T x  T2 $1 $] T2" (mangled, placeholder re-inserted and template tail duplicated). The mangled prompt is fed straight to runCodex, so the model reviews corrupted context and the resulting verdict/findings are presented as authoritative.

findings.title: String.replace reinterprets `$` in bundle JSON, findings, and patch
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace(search, replaceValue)` applies special `$` patterns when replaceValue is a string: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched sentinel, `` $` ``→everything before the match, `$'`→everything after the match, `$1`/`$<name>`→capture refs. The base code deliberately passed a function (`() => JSON.stringify(...)`, `() => bundle.patch`) precisely so the replacement is inserted verbatim (a function's return value is never pattern-expanded). Lines 25, 32, and 33 now pass raw strings, so any `$&`, `$'`, `` $` ``, `$$`, or `$1` inside `bundle`, `candidate`, or `bundle.patch` is rewritten. `bundle.patch` is the arbitrary unified diff under review and routinely contains `$` (shell, regex, template literals, jQuery), so the critic prompt gets corrupted content — e.g. a `$&` in the patch re-inserts the literal `{{PATCH}}` sentinel, and a `$'` duplicates the tail of critic.md. This is silent: no error is raised, the corrupt prompt is sent to the model, and the returned review is wrong.

findings.title: String replace arg re-expands `$` patterns in bundle/patch
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the replacement argument from a function (`() => JSON.stringify(...)`, base lines 25/32/33) to a plain string makes `String.prototype.replace` interpret `$$`, `$&`, `` $` `` and `$'` (and `$n`) in the replacement value. Those sequences appear routinely in code diffs/reviewed source (e.g. `.replace(x, "$&")`, Makefile/shell `$$`, bash `$'...'`). When present in `JSON.stringify(bundle)` (line 25), the candidate findings JSON (line 32), or especially `bundle.patch` (line 33, raw diff), the injected text is rewritten — `$&` becomes the literal match marker `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}`, `` $` ``/`$'` splice in surrounding prompt text, and `$$` collapses to `$`. The model then reviews a corrupted bundle/patch, silently producing wrong findings/verdict. The previous function form inserted the string verbatim.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output instead of silently coercing
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview lost its `strict = true` default (base f6c13ac:137,155-165). In base, the default path called normalizeFinding, which threw on any malformed finding, so normalizeReview rejected the whole review on invalid model output. HEAD always runs `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` (schema.ts:131) and normalizeFinding no longer throws (schema.ts:95-110), so malformed output such as `{findings:[{severity:'critical'}]}` now returns a RawReview containing a fabricated finding (severity 'P1', category 'bug', file '', lineStart 0) rather than raising a validation error. Every consumer of the exported normalizeReview is now forced onto the lenient path with no way to request strict validation; the 'reject bad review output' contract no longer exists.

findings.title: Keep rejecting malformed findings instead of coercing defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Every malformed-field guard was deleted and replaced with silent defaults: invalid severity is coerced to "P1" (line 98), missing/invalid category to "bug" (lines 100-102), missing file to "" (line 103), and missing or non-numeric lineStart/lineEnd to 0 or NaN (lines 104-105). Where the body previously threw (e.g. `throw new Error('malformed finding: invalid severity ...')`) so garbled model output surfaced as an error, callers now receive a fabricated but structurally-valid Finding reporting a P1 at file "" line 0 (NaN serializes to null), and can no longer distinguish failed output from a real finding.

findings.title: Restore strict-mode rejection removed from normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `normalizeReview(raw: any, strict = true)` promised that malformed findings abort the review by default; it is now `normalizeReview(raw: any)` and the findings map (line 131) is unconditionally lenient. Callers relying on the default strict rejection silently lose it, and callers that passed `strict=false`—whose invalid findings were previously dropped (catch -> null -> filter)—now instead receive the coerced, defaulted findings from normalizeFinding. The contract and both call patterns changed without the body implementing the removed guarantee.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently fabricates defaults for malformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: Every failure signal this function used to raise was replaced with a coercing default: invalid/unknown severity -> "P1" (line 98), invalid category -> "bug" (lines 100-102), missing file -> "" (line 103), missing/invalid lineStart -> Number(...); a non-numeric lineStart (e.g. "abc") becomes NaN (line 104), lineEnd likewise (line 105), and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix/validation are accepted (lines 107-109). These are exactly the branches the base version threw on (git show 0719f51:src/shared/schema.ts). A reviewer/UI consuming the result can no longer distinguish "the model emitted a malformed finding" from "a real P1 finding at file ''/line 0"; it will render/bill/report the fallback as real. Additionally the `!raw || typeof raw !== "object"` guard was removed, so normalizeFinding(null) now throws a bare TypeError instead of the previous explicit Error. This is an exported function, so the strip-mined error contract is the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: normalizeReview no longer fails closed on malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The `strict = true` parameter was dropped and the strict ternary at line 131 replaced with `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)`. Previously a malformed finding either aborted the whole review (strict, the default) or was filtered out (strict=false). Now, because normalizeFinding never rejects, malformed findings are silently retained as fabricated P1/"bug" entries with file "" and line 0/NaN, and no caller can request fail-closed behavior anymore. A review payload that is corrupt, or partially hallucinated, is therefore reported as a valid review containing real-looking P1 findings rather than being rejected.

findings.title: Restore -R repo flag: refs step runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (lines 26-40) executes BEFORE 'Checkout PR head' (lines 42-46), so at the time these gh calls run there is no guaranteed git remote in the working directory. Dropping `-R "$REPO"` makes gh fall back to inferring the repo from the cwd's git remotes; on a fresh/clean self-hosted workspace (first run, ephemeral runner, or after workspace cleanup) there is no remote, so `gh pr view` fails with 'failed to determine base repo'. Because bash -e does not treat a failure inside `$( )` within `echo` as fatal (verified: `bash -e -c 'echo "x=$(false)"'` exits 0), the step still succeeds and writes empty head/base — actions/checkout then falls back to the default ref and PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA are empty, so the review targets the wrong SHAs. This only affects workflow_dispatch, i.e. the manual trigger the input was added for.

findings.title: Restore repo flag: gh pr view runs before checkout with no git remote
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step (line 26) executes before `actions/checkout` (line 42), so the workspace has no git remote and no `GH_REPO` env is set anywhere in the job. In the old code `-R "$REPO"` (`${{ github.repository }}`) let `gh` operate without a checkout; removing it means `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` cannot determine the repository and exits non-zero. That non-zero exit is hidden because the call sits inside `$(...)` in an `echo`, so `set -e`/`pipefail` never see it: the step still succeeds and writes `head=` / `base=` empty to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`. The only path through this branch is `workflow_dispatch` (pull_request sets EVENT_HEAD and takes the `if` branch), so manual reviews then pass an empty ref to `actions/checkout` (falls back to the default branch) and empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA to the reviewer, i.e. the wrong revision pair is reviewed (or the job fails on a cold runner).

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view on workflow_dispatch path
findings.whyItBreaks: This step runs before the `actions/checkout` at line 42, so `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` is not a git repository on a cold runner. `gh pr view` resolves the target repo only from `GH_REPO` or the cwd's git remote (verified empirically: gh 2.98.0 ignores `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, and with no checkout it exits 1 with `fatal: not a git repository`). Dropping `-R "$REPO"` therefore removes the only deterministic repo specifier. Because the call sits inside `echo "head=$(...)"`, gh's non-zero exit is swallowed and the step still succeeds with `head=`/`base=` empty; `actions/checkout` at line 42-46 then checks out the default ref and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` are empty, so the review runs against the wrong revision (or fails) instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Parse candidate review strictly; lenient mode drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The added second argument selects normalizeReview's non-strict mode, which wraps normalizeFinding in try/catch and filters out every finding that fails validation (missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, invalid severity/category, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd) instead of throwing. The guard immediately below only checks `summary` and `checked.length`, so it does not detect the dropped findings; the shrunken candidate is then serialized into the critic prompt (src/core/review.ts:35) and can also back-fill `checked`/`summary` (src/core/review.ts:47,49). Result: a run whose model output was malformed completes as a valid review and can report `pass`, having silently discarded a finding the model actually produced — failure is indistinguishable from a legitimately short findings list. The sibling critic parse at src/core/review.ts:38 deliberately keeps the strict default, which shows the intent of strict parsing and makes the candidate-specific loosening the outlier.

findings.title: Restore strict parsing of the candidate pass; loose mode drops findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw) defaults to strict mode: it validates each finding and throws on a malformed one, which previously aborted review() loudly. Passing `false` switches to loose mode, where each malformed finding is caught and filtered out (mapped to null + removed) with no log and no signal. The only downstream gate is `!candidate.summary || candidate.checked.length === 0` (line 30), which passes when a finding was dropped. The critic is fed solely from candidate via `{{FINDINGS}}` (line 35) and the returned findings come only from pruned (lines 43-49), so a candidate finding with a single malformed required field (e.g. missing suggestedFix or bad severity) can never resurface and deriveVerdict can return `pass` instead of `changes_requested`. Failure is no longer distinguishable from a legitimately empty findings list.

findings.title: Restore fail-fast validation in normalizeReview (silently coerces bad output)
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, normalizeReview threw for non-object input, a non-string summary, and missing/non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks (see git show 1439b29:src/shared/schema.ts:115-131). The new body coerces every malformed shape into a valid-looking empty RawReview: raw=null/non-object yields summary '', findings [], checked [], residual_risks []; a real object missing findings likewise yields []. Callers of this exported function can no longer distinguish a failed/unparseable model response from a legitimate zero-finding review, so a malformed review can be rendered/persisted/reported as an empty passing review — a silent loss of the previous error signal.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-output errors into empty defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deleted every validation throw (base: src/shared/schema.ts:115-131) and replaced failures with silent fallbacks: non-object/missing-field input now yields summary '', findings [], checked [], residual_risks [] instead of raising. Because an empty review is a legitimate value (a passing review with no findings), every caller is forced to conflate a malformed/absent model response with a real clean review, and can persist/report a failed run as a pass. The signal is not logged and not otherwise distinguishable, so the previously-observable failure path is gone.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed review output as an empty valid review
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously every structural failure was a hard error: non-object input, non-string summary, or missing findings/checked/residual_risks threw `malformed review output: ...` and the failure reached the caller. The new body maps each of those to a benign default (`summary: ""`, `findings: []`, `checked: []`, `residual_risks: []`), so a truncated, parse-failed, or schema-mismatched model response is returned as a successful `RawReview` with zero findings. Any caller that derives a verdict from `findings.length === 0` / empty `summary` will report a clean PASS for a review that never actually ran, and the exception path that previously surfaced the failure is removed. The contract is exported (public surface), so the ambiguity is baked into the API: every caller is forced to conflate "model produced garbage" with "review completed, nothing found".

findings.title: Do not downgrade errored review check from failure to neutral

GitHub treats a neutral conclusion as non-blocking for a required status check (same as success/skipped), and neutral is also the legitimate value emitted for the needs_human verdict (VERDICT_CONCLUSION at src/adapters/github.ts:50-54). A consumer enforcing the Needlefish check therefore can no longer distinguish 'review crashed' from 'review ran and was neutral', so a PR whose review errored becomes mergeable — the exact failure signal the check exists to raise is swallowed.

findings.title: Keep failed-review check blocking instead of neutral

findings.title: Errored review posts passing-equivalent "neutral" check, unblocking merge

GitHub evaluates required status checks / check runs with conclusion success, skipped, or neutral as PASSING, whereas "failure" blocks. So when `review(bundle)` throws (model/API/transport error), the Needlefish check goes green in the merge box and a required-check branch protection rule no longer blocks the PR — even though the very same payload (line 193) says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." The failure signal is silently downgraded to a value indistinguishable from the legitimate `needs_human` neutral state (VERDICT_CONCLUSION.needs_human at line 53), so consumers cannot tell 'review could not run' from 'review ran, needs human'. findings.title: Restore case/whitespace normalization for severity input
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` used to canonicalize the incoming severity before matching. Now `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` compares the raw value directly, so any non-canonical but valid severity (e.g. "p1", " P1 ", "p0") fails the guard and is silently reclassified to the fallback (`P3`). A model/harness emitting lowercase severities previously produced "P1"/"P2" and now produces "P3", misclassifying real blocking findings as lowest severity on a live path (normalizeReview -> normalizeFinding).

findings.title: Unknown-severity fallback downgraded from P1 to P3 (fail-open)
findings.whyItBreaks: When severity is missing or unrecognized the function previously defaulted to `P1`, keeping unknown findings in the high-severity band. It now defaults to `P3`, the least severe band, so malformed/model-drifted severities are silently downgraded and no longer surface as blocking. This is a fail-open change: an unparsable value is indistinguishable from a legitimate low-severity finding at the point callers read `Finding.severity`.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization and stop downgrading unknowns to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code did `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` then `SEVERITIES.includes(sev) ? sev : "P1"`. The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` with no trim/uppercase and defaults to "P3". Substituting real inputs: `{severity:"p0"}`, `{severity:" p1 "}` (LLM output is routinely lower-cased or padded) now fail the case/whitespace-sensitive `includes` and fall through to "P3" instead of being preserved as P0/P1; any unrecognized value (e.g. "critical", garbage) is likewise downgraded from the old "P1" to "P3". Since Finding.severity drives downstream verdict/blocking behavior, a genuine P0/P1 defect is relabelled as low-risk P3 and can ship — a real severity-misclassification regression, not just cosmetic.

findings.title: Restore case/whitespace normalization of severity in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and matched that against SEVERITIES. The new code feeds `raw.severity` straight into `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)`, so any value that is not already one of the exact uppercase literals now misses the match and falls to the fallback. Concretely `"p2"`, `" P0 "`, or `"p3\n"` returned their normalized severity before and now return the fallback. Because `normalizeFinding` consumes untyped model/JSON output (`normalizeReview` maps `raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)` at src/shared/schema.ts:132), non-canonical casing/whitespace is exactly the input the removed `.trim().toUpperCase()` existed to absorb, and a real P0/P1 finding is silently reclassified as the default. The fallback also changed from "P1" to "P3" (lowest severity), so the misrouted values land on the least-significant severity instead of a mid/high one, hiding the signal further.

findings.title: Stop leaking GitHub tokens into spawned codex process env
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version built `env = { ...process.env }`, deleted `GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_API_TOKEN`, and passed `env` to `spawnSync`. This diff removes both the deletions and the `env` option. Node's `spawnSync` inherits `process.env` when `env` is omitted, so the spawned `codex exec` agent process (an AI agent running `-s read-only` in the target repo, potentially with network access) now receives live GitHub credentials in its environment. On any host/CI where `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` is set (the normal case this repo is a PR-review runner), those tokens are exposed to the sub-process, undoing a deliberate secret-scrubbing guard.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing for spawned codex process
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change `runCodex` built a sanitized env (`{ ...process.env }` minus GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN) and passed it as the `env` option to spawnSync. The diff deletes both the sanitized env construction and the `env` option, so spawnSync (env omitted) falls back to inheriting the full parent environment. The child process is `codex exec` — an LLM agent run that can spawn tool subprocesses — which now receives live GitHub credentials that were intentionally withheld. This silently removes the credential-isolation control the original code existed to provide.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR deletes the `env` construction and the three `delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN` lines and drops `env` from the spawnSync options. With no `env` option, Node's child_process defaults to the parent's full `process.env`, so the spawned `codex exec` process (which is fed the untrusted prompt/PR text and runs with network access) now inherits any GitHub credentials present in the environment. The read-only sandbox only restricts the filesystem, not network egress or `gh`/API auth, so the reviewed agent can exfiltrate or act on those tokens. Removal of a deliberate secret boundary is a supply-chain/credential-exposure regression, not a cleanup.

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing limiting this `pull_request` job to same-repo branches. With it gone, the job now runs for PRs whose head repo is a fork. `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18) means attacker-controlled fork code executes on your self-hosted infrastructure: `actions/checkout` pulls `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 23), `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs the fork's package.json install/lifecycle scripts (line 28), and `tsx src/cli.ts` runs the fork's own CLI with a `GH_TOKEN` in env (lines 32-34). Any external contributor can therefore achieve arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted runner by opening a PR, reaching internal network resources and any persistent runner state. (For public-repo fork PRs the token is read-only, but that does not mitigate the RCE on self-hosted hardware.)

findings.title: Removing fork-PR guard runs untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only barrier preventing this job from executing for fork-originated PRs. With it gone, the `pull_request` trigger (opened/synchronize/reopened) runs the job on a `self-hosted` runner for any fork. The job then (1) checks out the PR head ref (fork-controlled code), (2) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` — which executes arbitrary lifecycle/postinstall scripts from the fork's manifest — and (3) executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` with `GH_TOKEN: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` and `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` permissions. A self-hosted runner is persistent and typically holds other credentials/artifacts, so a malicious fork PR can exfiltrate runner secrets or poison the runner for subsequent trusted builds — exactly the scenario the removed guard existed to prevent.

findings.title: Removing fork guard lets untrusted PRs run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing keeping fork-originated PRs off this job. Without it, `pull_request` events from any fork now schedule the job on `runs-on: self-hosted` (review.yml:18), which then checks out the fork's code at `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (review.yml:23) and runs `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (review.yml:28). pnpm install executes the fork's package.json dependency lifecycle scripts (preinstall/install/postinstall), i.e. arbitrary code supplied by an external contributor runs on Frank's self-hosted machine; the subsequent `tsx src/cli.ts` step executes the fork's own source. `--frozen-lockfile` only pins dependency versions, it does not prevent the fork from adding lifecycle scripts or changing source. `pull_request` (not `pull_request_target`) does keep repo secrets/GITHUB_TOKEN read-only for forks, but that does not protect the runner host itself, which may hold credentials, SSH keys, or the .needlefish working state.

findings.title: Do not silently override a valid 0ms runner duration with the fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, readRunnerDurationMs("0", fallback) returned 0; with `parsed > 0` it now returns fallbackMs. The two live consumers parse env values at src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-5 (NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS, fallback 5000) and :7-9 (NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS, fallback 2000), and their results drive the escalation timers at :124 (SIGTERM->SIGKILL grace) and :123 (post-SIGKILL give-up). A user who deliberately sets either var to 0 (e.g. `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` to skip the graceful period and escalate straight to SIGKILL, or `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` to stop waiting for close immediately) is silently ignored and gets 5000ms / 2000ms instead, with no warning or doc note. 0 is a legal millisecond duration for setTimeout, so the previous `>= 0` behavior was correct; the tightened predicate introduces a config-value regression rather than rejecting malformed input.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration now silently replaced by larger default
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate was tightened from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. The only behavioral delta is the value 0: Number("0") = 0 was previously honored (enabling an immediate SIGKILL escalation / immediate give-up), but now falls through to `fallbackMs`. A user who explicitly sets NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now gets 5000ms of grace instead of 0 (src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-6), and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now gets 2000ms (src/shared/runner-process.ts:7-10). Both feed the live kill timers at src/shared/runner-process.ts:124 and src/shared/runner-process.ts:123, so process-termination timing changes for that config. The new guard's stated intent (finite/non-negative) does not require rejecting 0, and 0 causes no runtime error at those setTimeout sites, so the rejection is an unintended over-block.

findings.title: Guard now silently overrides explicit 0 grace/give-up config
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs is the parser for two operator-facing env configs (NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS @src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-6, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS @src/shared/runner-process.ts:7-10). Substitution: value="0" → trimmed="0" (not undefined/"") → parsed=0 → guard `parsed > 0` @:135 evaluates false → returns fallbackMs. Pre-change `parsed >= 0` returned 0. So a user who set 0 to mean "no grace / kill immediately" now silently gets the default 5000ms (grace) or 2000ms (give-up) at the live call sites @src/shared/runner-process.ts:124 and :123, changing real kill timing despite an explicit setting. This is an over-blocking tightening of a config predicate.

findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block computed the changed files absent from every selected hotspot and appended them as a 'tail-coverage' hotspot to guarantee each changed file got deep-reviewed. Head now only iterates `hotspots = sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93): any changed file the map pass did not assign to a surface, and any hotspot ranked below the top 6, is never passed to a deep pass and contributes neither a finding nor a residual_risks entry. reviewLarge can therefore return a PASS verdict for a large PR whose changed files were never reviewed at all.

findings.whyItBreaks: The loop no longer accumulates each deep pass's `res.residual_risks` (the `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` line was deleted) and line 113 hard-codes `residual_risks: []` on the candidate handed to the critic. A blocking gap found during a deep pass can be silently cleared and the review can pass.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so every changed file is deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now takes only `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (MAX_HOTSPOTS = 6, src/core/review.ts:23) and then immediately builds the deep prompts from that truncated list. The removed tail-coverage block used to compute files not covered by any selected hotspot and push a `tail-coverage` hotspot, so every changed file still got a deep pass. The map pass runs with no diff text (mapBundle omits `patch`, src/core/review.ts:80-86), so any changed file ranked below the top 6 or not mapped to a surface is now never deep-reviewed and the review can emit PASS for files it never opened — exactly the case the removed comment ("never silently skip a changed file") guarded against.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so every changed file is deep-reviewed

That block is deleted, and nothing else covers unmapped files: the deep prompt is built from {{HOTSPOT}} only (lines 98-100), and the map pass (map.md) may return hotspots that do not mention every changed path. findings.title: Removing the {{FOCUS}} substitution silently drops the focus hint from deep passes

If `deep.md` still declares `{{FOCUS}}` (it must, or the deleted replace was dead code), the deep-review prompt now ships an unsubstituted literal token and `bundle.focus` — a caller-supplied option — is never applied, so large-PR deep reviews silently ignore the requested focus with no error or residual risk recorded. findings.title: formatDuration can render '60s' or 'Xm 60s' after remainder rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored and seconds are rounded independently, so a remainder of 59.5s+ rounds up to 60 and is never carried into the minute. The old code rounded total seconds first (totalSeconds = Math.round(ms/1000)), so totalSeconds % 60 was always < 60. Concretely, ms=119500 now yields minutes=1 and seconds=Math.round(59.5)=60 -> '1m 60s' (old: '2m 0s'), and ms=59999 yields minutes=0, seconds=Math.round(59.999)=60 -> '60s' (old: '1m 0s'), making the output inconsistent with ms=60000 -> '1m 0s'. These values are reached from the real call sites at render.ts:75 (per-call durationMs) and render.ts:80 (totalDurationMs).

findings.title: formatDuration can render a '60s' seconds component
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes and seconds are now computed independently: minutes = floor(ms/60000) and seconds = round((ms%60000)/1000). Whenever the sub-minute remainder is >= 59500ms, the seconds component rounds up to 60 while minutes is not incremented, so the function returns a non-normalized string such as '1m 60s' (ms=119999 -> minutes=1, seconds=round(59999/1000)=60) or '60s' (ms=59999) instead of '2m 0s'/'1m 0s'. The pre-PR code derived minutes from the already-rounded total seconds (floor(totalSeconds/60), totalSeconds%60), so the seconds component was always in 0..59 and '60s' was impossible. The output is user-visible in the rendered review stats line (src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80).
